The rites, rituals beliefs, practices and languages make tribals different from other communities. 7ripura tribe is one of the major tribes in terms of their number and distribution in the state. 7ripura tribe is quite different from other two tribes- namely Debbarma & Murasingh of Tripuri Community. The present volume is an effort to focus the status of Tripura tribes in the light of both historical and modern time. It is very good research document about their demographic, anthropological and socio-economic status. This isa commendable effort of the authors. It would surely be useful for those who are interested to know about the Tripura tribes and also for those who want to conduct further study in future. We wish a great success of this scholarly work. ethnological segment in the Indian population. The existence of the tribals in India has been recorded long before the penetration of Aryan speaking people who came to India following some ethnic upheaval or changes of climate in Central Asia. Numerically Tripura are the largest tribe of Tripura. Tripura tribe is a sub-division of Boro group of languages of Tibete-Chinese family. The book comprises five chapters. FIRST CHAPTER is about general introduction of Tribes and Scheduled Tribes in India. It reviews the concept of Tribes and Scheduled Tribes given by various scholars and discusses geographical concentration of Scheduled Tribes in different regions in India. The chapter also introduces the state Tripura with historical and sociological references. SECOND CHAPTER presents demographical profiles of different Tribes and specially Tripura Tribes in Tripura based on secondary data available under Census of India in different years. Some of the information was recorded even before the starting of census operation in India. It gives a clear transition of Tribals in Tripura over the passage of time. THIRD CHAPTER is an anthropological journey on Life and Culture of Tripura Tribe (whose who are writing Tripura as surname) of Tripuri Community in brief. This chapter has been prepared based on the literature review, in depth field study and discussion with the aged and learner persons of Tripura tribes. The major objective for preparation of the chapter was to highlight only those issues which support a different identity of Tripura tribes from other two tribes namely Debbarma and Murasingh of Tripura Community. FORTH CHAPTER is a Bird View of present status of Tripura tribe in Tripura. This is an intensive study or may say as acomplete enumeration through out

the state covering all the districts, blocks, Gram Panchayats, Villages and even hamlets where Tripura tribes are habiting. This chapter brings the block wise distribution of Tripura tribe and its clan, Age wise distribution, educational and occupational status, availabilities of basic infrastructure and development efforts in their habitats. FIFTH CHAPTER is a Worm View of present status of Tripura Tribe in Tripura. This is an empirical study with a small sample size. The chapter presets household level information on different socio-economic issues. Some relevant Annexure which gives the detail list of habitats of Tripura tribes through out the state at the end of the book enriched the book. This will be helpful not only for the policymakers but also for the researchers interested for further work on Tripura tribes. We are indebted to Shri. Tribal society is referred to as ‘primitive society’ or ‘pre-state society’, or ‘folk society’ or even as ‘simple society’. Sometimes, the word ‘tribe’ is taken as a synonym of the term race but scientifically ‘race’ carries an entirely different meaning. However, all these terms indicate that the tribals are the backward group in comparison to other advanced social groups. But unfortunately there was no commonly accepted definition of

this word. INTRODUCTION A tribe is an anthropological concept. It is referred to by certain authors as ‘animistic’ or ‘aboriginal’. The term ‘Adivasi’ has gained popularity while referring to the tribe in recent years. Tribals are thought of as semi-civilized people residing in hills, forests or considered as special groups of agriculturists. A tribe is generally defined as a social group usually living in a definite area, having a dialect, cultural homogeneity and unified social organization. According to the Oxford Dictionary, “a tribe is a group of people in a primitive or barbarous stage of development acknowledging the authority ofa chiefand usually regarding them as having a common ancestor”. Identification of tribes in India became extremely difficult as various types of social groups appeared in association with tribes. Among these diversified social groups, castes created principal hindrance. Many tribes were described as castes and many castes were labeled as tribes as well. Evolutionist thinkers of nineteenth century first attempted to distinguish the tribal societies. They focused on the legal and political institutions. Some scholars regarded those societies as tribals who exhibited social institutions but lacked political one. Henry Maine (1861), on the other hand, found the distinction in legal terms. The modern usage of the term ‘tribe’ suggests that it is a small-scale social grouping that display some form of cultural unity. The members recognize a close affinity towards one another. A compact and self-sufficient economy is found in such groups unlike the modern society. Within the spatial and temporal range of social, legal and political relations, they possess a morality, religion and a world-view of corresponding dimensions. Although tribal societies are supremely ethno-centric, but a tribe is no longer

referred to in terms of its cultural homogeneity. India has the largest tribal population in the world. It is equal to the sum total of tribal population of nineteen other countries. According to 2001 census, India has a tribal population of 84.3 million, which constitute 8.2 percent of the total population of India. The tribal population of India is more than the total population of France and Britain and four times that of Australia. Ifall the tribals of India had lived in one state it could be the fifth most populous state after Uttar Pradesh, Bihar. West Bengal and Maharashtra. The tribal people are the oldest ethnological segment in

the Indian population. The existence of the tribals in India has been recorded long before the penetration of Aryan speaking people who came to India following some ethnic upheaval or changes of climate in Central Asia. The scientists trace the origin of Indian tribals to three roots: the Negrito, the Proto- Astraloid and the Mongoloid. The tribal with Proto-Astroloid root form one major group who came from the basin of Mediterranean sea and established themselves in Central & Eastern part of India. A later swarm of Aryan groups in the mountainous regions which lacked communication facilities and amenities of daily life. The tribals put a brave front to all the calamities and inhospitalities of man and nature and tried to retain their unique identity and simplicity. In the past from 1774 to 1919 some British administrators and missionaries, travelers and a few others who were oriented towards anthropology observed and described the life and culture of different tribal and rural groups. Some people prepared detailed accounts as specific tribes and castes. This was a sort of formative phase for tribal researchers in India. From 1920 to 1949, known as a constructive period of tribal research trained scholars like Ghurye (1942 and 1946), Mazumder (1937), Karve (1940-41), Bose (1948) and some foreign scholars like Elwin (1939 and 1942) and Furer-Haimendorf (1943) took up specialized subjects like kinship studies and social organization of tribals for research. The third phase of tribal research was known as analytical period, which started from 1950. In this period systematic analytical and action-oriented studies of Indian villages and tribal areas were and are being undertaken by scholars like Mazumder (1963) Berreman (1963 and 1964), Sinha (1962), Vidyarthi

(1965) and others. Among them, Burlings (1963) was the first to publish a village study on a tribe in India. A condensed review of these research studies suggests the presence of some efforts, though insufficient towards understanding tribals in different parts of India. But there are still some tribes, which have somehow evaded the attention of many sociologists and anthropologists. Among them one of the least studied tribe is the Halam tribe residing in the North-East region (Tripura). The difficulties of communication facilities with plains have kept the Halam isolated from the mainstream to a large extent. Asa result, they still havea distinct cultural setup and socio-economic structure. But they came in contact with Christian missionaries, and became converted and have changed their religion. In the North-East corner of India, Tripura is a tiny and hilly state. According to the former president of India Mr. R. Venkatraman, Tripura is the gem of brilliant necklace of India. Its ae wee eee population is heterogeneous. Diverse ethnic elements can be traced in it. Thus, Tripura is a fertile field to study Anthropology and Sociology for its colorful tribes like Tripura, Riang, Chakma, Jamatia, Noatia, Mog, Halam, Uchai, Kuki and so on. Among the Indian states Tripura is by far the most ancient. The state has numerous vicissitudes of time, been able to maintain its individuality and integrity up to the present time. The Mahabharata and Puranas show that this state was established 3000 years before Christ. Rajmala, the historical chronicle of the later king of Tripura, says that the king of this state took up arms on behalf of Duryyodhana against the Pandavas at the famous battle of Kurukshetra. According to written

documents of Rajmala, the history of Tripura began with the settlement of Yayati’s exiled son Druhya. The great king Yayati of the Lunar dynasty had five sons, namely Yadu, Turvasu, Druchyu, Anu and Puru by two wives, Devayani, daughter of Sukracharya and Sarmistha, daughter of Vrishaprava. Sanskrit Raj mala and Raja Ratnakar describe the victorious career of Druhya which indicates that after leaving the capital Prathisthanpur, he proceeded along the banks of the Ganges towards the sea and came across a beautiful island name “Sagar” just at the confluence of the Bhagirathi and the sea where he set up his suzerainty. In course of time he extended his kingdom and brought several neighboring rulers under his way. Kalidasa’s “Meghaduta” also contains a reference to Tripura in the following words, “There the bamboos, as they are filled with the wind, produce pleasing sounds while the victory over Tripura is sung in chorus by the wives of the Kinnaras. In older times, it extends in the north to Kamrup and in the east to Arakan. Ralph Fitch, who traveled through the country in 1585, noted that ‘the kings of Tippara had almost continual wars with the Arakanese’ and that their military prestige was at its height during that century. In the 18" century, the whole territory fell to the Nawab of Murshidabad. On assuming control of this area. the British allowed the state to hold its territories in the hills while recognizing the Rajah’s title to the Zamindari in the plains. Thus the Tripura Maharaja was both a British India Zamindar and a ruling Prince.” According to B.P.Mishra (1976) the territory was known as “Hill Tippera” before 1920 and it was distinguished

from the neighbouring “Tipperah” which constituted one of the districts of British India in the lower plains of East Bengal. But, since that year, on the representation of the durbar, the Government of British India agreed that the state should be known as “Tripura” instead of “Hill Tippera” (Memoranda on the Indian ° states,1932,p.218). According to Mahadev Chakraborty (1990) the state was formerly known as “Swadhin Tripura” and later on as “Hill Tippera” till 1920 when its name was changed to “Tripura”. The name “Tripura” has been derived from Zripura Sundari, the main deity of the land (Hunter, 1876). Some believe that the name Tripura has been derived from two Tripura words viz. “Tui” and “pra”; “Tui” means “water” and “pra” means “near”. According to R.M Nath (1948) Tipperah people preferred to call themselves the children of water goddess and were, therefore, known as the Tipperahs. Some other believes that the word “Tripura” has been sanskritised which originated from “Tipra”, a native tribe of Tripura. Some people think that the name Tripura derived from “Tripuram” meaning “a land of three cities” or “three filled up substance”. Again some believe that a mythical king Tripur had named his kingdom “Tripura” after his own name. In Tripura, there are Indo-Aryan (Bengali) and Indo-Mongaloyed (Tripura, Reang, Debbarma, Jamatia, Noatia, Halam, Chakma, Mog, Kuki, Lushai and so on.) people. Besides the above said tribes, there are the Khasi, Garo, Bhutiya, Lepeha, Oraon, Munda, Santal, Bhil, Chaimal, Kunda or Kaur tribes in Tripura. There are also non tribal peo other than Bengalee like Nepali, Bihari and Assamese and others. It is very difficult to explain about the first settlers in this region .Because the written

document about the earliest human migration and movement in this region is not abundant. In all likelihood, peoples swamped here from North- East, South- East and West. The Burmese speaking people came from the south east and extended their settlement in the southern part. The Tibeto-Burman speaking people came from the North- East and settled in the North eastern hilly tracts. The Bengalee Hindus came from the west and crossed the river Meghna and settled along the narrow strip of valley. When the Tripura community appeared here, they were by no means the first peoples to have settled themselves in this tract. But it is difficult to trace the foot prints of the first group of settlers in the successive migratory waves .Out of those early settlers, at least five communities stood out prominently. Among them, the Bengalee in the West, the Tipra in the North East, the Mogh in the South, the Reang in the South-East, and the Kuki-Halam in the East but all there five groups cannot be placed on the same footing so far as the date of establishment of their authority in Tripura is concerned . Discovery of several copper plates used as records of land grants made by the king of the Meghna valley is very significant. But such evidences in the case of the Mogh, the Reang and the Kuki-Halam group were not prominently found and their political organization did not develop here. Due to the absence of evidences only the Bengalee and the Tripra dynasty have achieved attention. TRIPURA TRIBE: DEMOGRAPHIC PROFILE Numerically Tripura are the largest tribe of Tripura. According to 1961 census, out of total population of 1.142.005 persons in the

Mursum (a dialect of Halam) with 4486 speakers. There were also some languages and dialects which are spoken by persons belonging to communities which have settled here atleast more than one generation ago. Geographically, the major inhabitants of Tripura Tribe are confined to some of the Sub-Divisions of Tripura state namely: (1) Sabroom (2) Belonia (3) Amarpur (4) Gandachera (5) Longtrai Valley (6) Kailachabér (7) Kanchanpur and (8) Sonamura. DRESS AND ORNAMENTS The Tripuras wear Ritrok and homemade gamsa Borok and a Head dress called Khoroksa. - They also wear their home made coat Typed shirts called Kubai-borok especially at the Jhumwork(Jhum). The women wear a traditional dress called RINAI and breast cloth called RISA. The Rinai of Fatung/Fadung Dopha is almost similar to the Pinon of Chakma women. The Rinai worn by unmarried women is known as Rinai Chongrong. The women are fond of ornaments which are mostly made of silver and beads. Some male would also wear ear rings and chain which is now hardly seen. Tripuras wear SURAM/SURANG(hairband), KUNCHI, MANDOLI,BALAKHUR(in hands). RITES AND RITUALS The Tripuras observe a lot of rites and rituals. They perform Puja in the name of good number of god and goddesses. The Ochai (Priest) conduct the whole ceremonies. BURASA MATAI is acommon Puja and is done in the name of Burasa (The old man who is the Chief of all deities).It is also performed before the beginning of the Jnum Cutting at the site of the

Jnum. The family concerned has to sacrifice chickens, piggy etc., as per affordability. The “Ker Puja” or Para Kermani is done collectively by the villagers. Originally all the god and goddesses are paid homage in this puja. It requires about 21 (twenty one) nos. of chickens and 01(one) goat or pig and it is performed for prosperity and safety from illness and any dangers. PARA KERMANI: It is to be performed by the members of clans and it once performed, none of the clan can perform the same puja for the next 07(seven) years. One high Bamboo is erected in the courtyard and the Ochai and his helper called Tan-chorai (who slaughters the sacrificial animals and birds as per the direction of the Ochai, who chant the Mantras) manage the whole ceremony. The erected bamboo is decorated with Risas and at least 14 chickens, pigs, goat and some time buffaloes are sacrificed in the name of deities. It is also required 7(seven) Bhati (used for making wine) of wine which are sacredly prepared and kept separate. One ‘bhati’ of wine is used for each deity namely (1) Khoroksonai Matai (god of head washing). (2) Hanokmano Janoknai Matai (god of universe and house hold) (3) Burasa (Chief ofall deities) (4) Twibukma (.water goddess) (5) Sang-grangma (wife of Burasa- the angriest ofall deities) (6) Boroi- sini/bailing-koton) (seven sisters) Salangtwi (goddess of stupidity) . Malangtwi (goddess of bluntness) Hogjakbi (goddess of greediness) Sakjukbi (goddess of carelessness) Baibari (goddess of teasing) _ Khamali (goddess of getting convinced easily) Hammali (goddess of making good) sya eae The Tripuras believe that all sort of diseases are controlled by these seven sisters. The ‘Mulamuli Khamani’ puja is

performed by the husband and wife when abortion or miss * carriage of child takes place or if child dies one after another. The puja is conducted in the deep forest and offered to a big tree. None of the articles used in the puja can be brought back home. The couple has to dance circling around the tree wearing leaves at their feet. After marriage is over the family ordinarily pay homage to another deity named Chumlai Matai (god of household and prosperity). The Mailungma Matai’ is also performed on other times. Apart from the aforesaid pujas, the Tripuras observe a traditional and very sacred festival called Bwisu/ BUISU festival. It is performed on the last two days of passing year and on the first day of the New Year precisely calling them Hari Buisu and Buisuma’and bisi Katal. On the day of Hari-Buisu, people bathe at the dawn and collect flowers for worship of god. The day of Buisuma is so sacred to the Tripuras that they engaged themselves in prayer to gods and serve cakes, Aowan (pithas), panchans etc. The juniors pay respect to the elders while visiting houses. | On the Bisi Katal day, the first day of the New Year, they invite each other for feast. Goats, chicken and pigs are slaughtered on this day in BisiKatalni Puja-i.e., Mailwkma puja and Tuibukma puja etc. Wine is also offered on this day to the elders of the village (as a token of respect). The new couples are to respect thes day to the elders of the village (as a token of respect). The new couples are to respectir parents and other elders by washing their feet

first and then help them bathe in the Machang courtyard called Nugul/Noksar. Of course the elders have to pay some tips to the couples called Borda in the Tripura Dialect. During the Buisu days (3 days) Mai - Mai-chwlui (Rice) are spread throughout the village in order to the feed the cocks and hens and other birds. All the servants and maids are allowed to enjoy during these days. Kherebai Dance (22 no. of items) are performed in the Buisu festival. BIRTH RITES ‘Aayuk Katharni’ puja and ‘Bithi Karmani’ puja are performed for safe delivery of the child. It is done at the Sth month at the stage of pregnancy of the mother. ‘AbalaKainya’ puja is also is also performed _ in the bank ofa river or stream when no child is born to a couple. After delivery of the child, it is however, compulsory for the women that she should not touch water pitchers including the cooking utensils and other till the umbilical cord is detached from the child. A separate fire place (Thapa) is prepared for by bringing a heap of earth. Then Sukoi, Kuchar (indigenous herb) and turmeric together with other medicines articles are mixed by the ‘Gumajwk’ (mid-wife) and the mother is purified with the same. She has to go the river with the mid-wife and birth for purification. A fter the lapse of aforesaid period (one month time) the mother again has to be purified and allowed to do the house- hold work. The head of the child is shaved after this he/she is named. DEATH RITES When a Tripura dies a ‘Khai-nok’ (bamboo cot) is mace as high as the height of the chest

ofa man. The death is bathed and given new cloths after which it is placed on the said “Khai -nok’. A chicken is killed by throwing on the ground at the feet of the dead and it is then cooked out side the house. Rice is also cooked separately ina typical bamboo-pipe called ‘Wasung’ ( bamboo culm).A bamboo ‘Miacham’ (Rice Plate) is typically made which differs from the common one. A full meal is offered at the feet of the death and is called ‘Taksa Maikhlai Ronai’. Beating of Kham (Drum) in the specific rhythmic sound is necessary for the purpose. The villagers and the relatives turn up to the scene. A thread called “Yahrai Sonai Khudung/ Kwthwi Yakhrai’ (Dead man’s bridge) is carried from the house of the dead to the place of cremation place. It is believed that the thread works as bridge between the departed soul and the living members of the family till the ‘Kothoi Mai Romani’ is finalized. The death is then is placed ina bamboo made chariot like structure. If _ itis without wheel, it is called ‘Mang-gui’ and if it is wheeled it is called “Ratha-Sonai’. The next day morning calcined bones are collected and thrown in the water (Holy River) and cremation field is washed and polished. HUK CHAMANI (SHIFTING CULTIVATION) The Shifting Cultivation mainly comprises three major activities namely: (a) Huk Rommani/Lowa Kaimani/Wakhak Kaimani (b) Huk Katal Chamani (c) Hapeng Kwcham Chamani 2.1 HOOK ROMMANI/LOWA KAIMANI/WAKHAK KAIMANI The term literary means “locating of suitable hillock (land) for shifting cultivation”. Before cultivation the cultivator go around the hillocks and locate the suitable area and mark a sign known as Lowa Kaimani or Wakhak Kaimani. Whoever marks the sign first will possess the soul authority to cultivate in this area and no any second party can cultivate the land. And despite of this if any other person/party tends to cultivate, then it will be treated as illegal and will have to return the Hook (Shum) to the first party by virtue of law. 2.2 HOOK KATAL CHAMANI The term literally means “Choosing

of New Location (land) for Shifting Cultivation”. After locating the new area Clause 2.1 is to be followed. People belonging to a particular area cannot cultivate into the area outside of their jurisdiction. And if any one breaks this law, he/she will be forced to leave the area by virtue of law. 2.3 HAPING KACHAM CHAMANI The term literally means “Cultivating in the old area/land”. Some of the rules and regulation governing this activity are: 1. The cultivable land is under the control of the first person who has cultivated that very piece of land (Hook) before any person and has the domination period of 4 (four) years, i.e., the person can cultivate the land on the fourth year even after keeping the land uncultivated for the last 3 years. 2. Ifthe person fails to cultivate the land on the fourth year due to unavoidable circumstances, then he has to inform the Roaja and can extend his domination by another year. Further failure will lead to lose of his domination and ownership upon the land. 3. The person canalso further possess the land for another 4(four) years if he allows any third party to cultivate the land on some conditions, before the expiry of his domination period. 4. And ifthe domination of the land expires and remains uncultivated for unknown period will automatically be the property of the village.
